newsitem.title: UK: Political risk is not dead, but it may move house.
newsitem.headline: Political risk is not dead, but it may move house.

text.p: Financial markets used to panic at a hint of political risk but in today's post cold war orthodoxy they play it much cooler. Perhaps too cool. Analysts warn that political risk is not dead, and could yet rear up again in the most unlikely places -- including the apparently rock steady core of Europe.
"The key thing is whether the disappearance of Clinton and Yeltsin would change the world," said Stephen Bell, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"And the truth is -- not very much."
In the 1980s, the lingering Cold War and worldwide economic recession (and frothy booms) provided a volatile mix for the markets.
But with the Soviet empire now fragmented and capitalist economic orthodoxy taking root across the world, financial markets have become increasingly inured to political shocks.

Analysts noted two early 1990s crises -- the coup which temporarily ousted then Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev and the Gulf War. In both cases, major market reactions were later judged to be overdone and were quickly reversed.
Now, U.S. bombing of Iraq or calls from top Russian politicians for Yeltsin to resign give only a faint boost to the dollar or gold -- usually safe-havens in times of crisis.
"Political risk is relevant, but the old days when you'd see five or even 10 big figures movement on dollar/mark -- those days are over," said Bell.
Analysts say two main factors have reduced markets' sensitivity to political turmoil.

"Since the fall of the Soviet Union, markets have been crying wolf about Russia, so the impact of every twist and turn in Russian politics is getting smaller," said Stuart Thomson, chief international economist at Nikko in London.

The second drive has come from major industrialised nations, growth in an economic consensus favouring low inflation, healthy growth and tolerance of a certain level of unemployment means even changes in government produce few economic moves.

"In Britain, for example, people now say the differences between the two main poltical parties are very small -- so the risk we would see a dramatic change in economic policy with a change in government are greatly reduced," said Nikko's Thomson.
"Its much in he same in the U.S.."

With bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank seeking to impose a core policy of fiscal austerity and export-led growth on the world's developing nations, that critical mass will increase, analysts said.
But this push for an all-embracing orthodoxy may turn out to be a double-edged sword. While the conformity spreads across the globe, political risk may reappear in Europe, analysts said.
"If you want to identify political risk in the next two to hree years, it lies not in Russia, but in western Europe," said Thomson.

The only economic game being played in Europe is the push towards closer integration and a single currency. Any threat to that, would leave a dangerous vacuum, economists said. "An awful lot in Europe hangs on EMU. And there is no "plan B" in countries like France, Italy, Spain, Belgium, even Germany ... its the dominant political issue for them," said DMG's Bell. If European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- scheduled to start in 1999 -- does go ahead, all well and good.
But if it dissolves before starting, or collapses soon afterwards, the bricks and mortar of the most prominent, if not the only, support for economic policy in Europe would crumble.
"If EMU went, it would remove a consensus amongst European parties that reflects a great deal of political influence on economic policies," said Bell.

Most of all, analysts warned against complacency, saying it would be dangerous for investors to treat the reduction of poltical risk asscociated with the old-style superpowers as a sign it has disappeared altogether.
DMG's Bell said that with "market-friendly politicians in place across the world," political risk was not being taken as seriously as it it should.
"That will change," he said. "Unemployment is Europe's biggest problem, political mistrust of the centre is the United States' biggest problem, and Japan has dramatic social change."
"At the moment all this is being suppressed. But people will get fed up. I see 1997 as quite a difficult year for the political world."
